title: The paper clip wire
pageIntro: Test the wire on the bench. Run both tests, then answer.
stem:
A steel paper clip is made from a piece of straight metal wire. The results of two tests on the wire are shown.

The metal wire can be formed into the shape of the paper clip without breaking because the wire is ______.
figure:
Test on the wireWhat happened
Load testIt held the load without breaking.
Bend testIt bent without breaking.
hints: Which of the two tests changed the shape of the wire?
The wire passed both tests. Only one of them is about turning a straight wire into a curved clip.
key: Strong answers the load test. Flexible answers the bend test. Shaping something is always a bending question.

options.pick: The wire did hold the load without breaking, and "strong" sounds like the safest word for metal.
options.why: Strong only means it can take a load without breaking. A ceramic tile passes the load test and still snaps the moment it is bent, so being strong cannot explain how the wire was shaped.
clash: Your results: the load test never changed the shape of the wire.

options.pick: Making a paper clip means bending the wire into curves, so look at the bend test: the wire bent without breaking.
options.why: Flexible means it can bend without breaking. Forming the clip is bending, and the wire came through the bend test in one piece.

options.pick: Metal does not absorb water, so "waterproof" is a true statement about the wire.
options.why: It is true, but it is not the reason. Nothing in this question involves water, so this property is not being used.

options.text: able to let light pass through it
options.pick: It is one of the five properties, and it is the only option left if the first three seem wrong.
options.why: How much light a material lets through has nothing to do with bending a wire into shape.

title: Describing material K
pageIntro: Material K has not been used yet. Run both tests on it, then describe it.
stem:
A strip of material K was tested. The results are shown.

Which statement describes material K?
figure:
Test on KWhat happened
Load testIt held the load without breaking.
Bend testIt snapped as soon as it was bent.
hints: Your two results are different. One passed and one failed.
Describe K in two halves: what the load test showed, then what the bend test showed.
key: A material can pass one test and fail the other. Always say which test you mean.

options.text: Material K is strong and flexible.
options.pick: K survived the load test, and a material that passes one test often feels like it would pass the other.
options.why: K snapped in the bend test, so it is not flexible. Passing the load test says nothing about bending.
clash: Your results: K snapped as soon as it was bent.

options.text: Material K is not strong but it is flexible.
options.pick: A material that breaks is easy to think of as weak, and "flexible" fills the other half.
options.why: This is the opposite of the results. K held the load, so it is strong. It was the bending that broke it, so it is not flexible.
clash: Your results: K held the load without breaking.

options.text: Material K is strong but not flexible.
options.pick: Take the two results one at a time: load test passed, bend test failed.
options.why: K held the load without breaking, so it is strong. It snapped when it was bent, so it is not flexible. Glass and ceramic behave like this.

options.text: Material K is neither strong nor flexible.
options.pick: K broke, so it seems to fail everything.
options.why: K only broke in the bend test. Snapping when bent shows it is not flexible; it does not show it is weak. It held the load, so it is strong.
clash: Your results: K held the load without breaking.

title: Choosing wire for a paper clip
pageIntro: Three wires, A, B and C. Run both tests on all three.
stem:
A paper clip has to be bent into shape and then hold a thick stack of paper tightly without breaking. Three wires, A, B and C, were tested.

Which wire is most suitable for making the paper clip?
figure:
WireLoad testBend test
Abroke under the loadbent without breaking
Bheld the load without breakingbent without breaking
Cheld the load without breakingsnapped as soon as it was bent
hints: The clip has two jobs: it must be bent into shape, and it must then hold paper without breaking. That is two properties.
key: When a job needs two properties, the material must pass both tests. One pass is never enough.

options.pick: A bends easily, which is what making a paper clip looks like.
options.why: A broke under the load. A clip made from A would come apart as soon as it gripped a thick stack of paper.
clash: Your results: A broke under the load.

options.pick: C is strong, and a clip has to be tough to hold paper.
options.why: C snapped when it was bent, so it could never be formed into a clip in the first place.
clash: Your results: C snapped as soon as it was bent.

options.pick: All three are wires, so all three could be made into a clip.
options.why: Only B passed both tests. A and C each failed a test the clip depends on.
clash: Your results: A broke under the load and C snapped when bent.

options.pick: List both jobs first, then find the wire that passed both tests.
options.why: B bent without breaking and held the load without breaking, so it can be shaped and then grip the paper.

title: A toy boat for the pool
pageIntro: Run the float test and the water test on all three materials.
stem:
The body of a toy boat must stay on the surface of the water and must not get soggy after a long time in the pool. Three materials, P, Q and R, were tested.

Which material is most suitable for the body of the toy boat?
figure:
MaterialFloat testWater test
Pstayed near the surfacedid not absorb water
Qsank to the bottomdid not absorb water
Rstayed near the surfaceabsorbed water, mass went up
hints: Two jobs again: stay at the surface, and do not absorb water.
One material floats but absorbs water. One does not absorb water but sinks. Only one does both.
key: Floating and being waterproof are two separate properties. A material can float and still absorb water.

options.pick: Check both tests and take the material that passed both.
options.why: P stayed near the surface and did not absorb water, so the boat stays up and does not get soggy.

options.pick: Q does not absorb water, so no water gets into the boat.
options.why: Q sank in the float test. A boat that does not absorb water is still no use at the bottom of the pool.
clash: Your results: Q sank to the bottom.

options.pick: R floats, and floating looks like the main job of a boat.
options.why: R absorbed water. Floating says nothing about absorbing water, and a boat made of R would become soggy, which the question says to avoid.
clash: Your results: R absorbed water and its mass went up.

options.pick: Both P and R floated, so either one would keep the boat up.
options.why: Floating is only one of the two jobs. R fails the water test, so only P passes both.
clash: Your results: R absorbed water and its mass went up.

title: A window pane for the classroom
pageIntro: Run the light test and the load test on all three materials.
stem:
A classroom window pane must let in as much daylight as possible and must not break when the wind pushes on it. Three materials, D, E and F, were tested.

Which material is most suitable for the window pane?
figure:
MaterialLight testLoad test
Dlet most light throughbroke under the load
Elet most light throughheld the load without breaking
Flet some light throughheld the load without breaking
hints: Two materials let most light through. Which of them also held the load?
A window that lets in light but breaks in the wind has failed one of its two jobs.
key: How much light passes through is a property of its own: most, some or no light. Check it alongside the other properties the job needs.

options.pick: D lets most light through, which is what a window is for.
options.why: D broke under the load, so it would not survive the wind pushing on it.
clash: Your results: D broke under the load.

options.pick: F is strong, and a window has to survive knocks.
options.why: F only lets some light through, so the classroom would be dim. The window must let in as much daylight as possible.
clash: Your results: F let only some light through.

options.pick: D and E both let most light through, so either would light the room.
options.why: Letting light through is only one of the two jobs. D broke under the load, so only E does both.
clash: Your results: D broke under the load.

options.pick: Take the two jobs together: most light through, and no breaking under a load.
options.why: E is the only material that passed both tests.

title: Fair test: two strips of one material
pageIntro: Both strips are cut from the same material M. One is thin and one is thick. Bend both and see what happens.
stem:
Two strips were cut from the same material M. One strip is thin and the other is thick. Both strips were bent. The results are shown.

Lindy wants to compare how flexible four different materials are. What must she keep the same for a fair test?
figure:
StripBend test
Thin strip of Mbent without breaking
Thick strip of Msnapped as soon as it was bent
hints: Same material, two different results. What was different about the two strips?
If thickness alone can change the result, what must be kept the same when four different materials are compared?
key: Only the type of material may change. Everything else that could affect the bending, such as size, thickness and how far it is bent, must be kept the same.

options.pick: Keeping something the same sounds like the right idea, and colour is easy to control.
options.why: Colour has no effect on whether a material bends without breaking, so controlling it does nothing to make the test fair.

options.text: The type of material in each strip
options.pick: The question says "keep the same", and the materials are what she is testing.
options.why: The type of material is the one thing that must change. It is what she is testing, so keeping it the same would leave nothing to compare.

options.text: The size and thickness of each strip, and how far each is bent
options.pick: Find what else could change the result, then keep all of it the same.
options.why: The bench showed that thickness alone changed the result for the same material. If the strips differ in size or are bent by different amounts, a difference in the result might come from that instead of the material.

options.text: Nothing. She can just bend each strip until it breaks.
options.pick: Each strip gets the same action, so it feels fair already.
options.why: Your two strips of M got the same action and still gave different results, because one was thicker. Without keeping thickness the same, the comparison tells you nothing about the materials.
clash: Your results: the same material M gave two different bend results.

title: Wrapping a sandwich
stem:
A sheet of aluminium foil can be folded tightly around a sandwich without breaking.

Which property of the foil makes this possible?
key: Folding and wrapping are bending jobs. Bending without breaking is flexibility.

options.pick: Foil that stays in one piece sounds tough, so "strong" seems to fit.
options.why: Strong means it can take a load without breaking. Nothing heavy is hanging on the foil here; it is being folded, which is bending.

options.pick: Foil keeps a sandwich from getting wet, so waterproof sounds useful.
options.why: That may be true, but the question is about folding the foil without breaking it. Waterproof is about not absorbing water, and folding does not test that.

options.text: It does not let light pass through.
options.pick: You cannot see through foil, which is a real property of foil.
options.why: True, but it has nothing to do with folding. Light is not part of this job.

options.pick: Folding is bending. Ask which property lets a material bend without breaking.
options.why: Flexible means it can bend without breaking, which is exactly what happens when the foil is folded around the sandwich.

title: Two strips, two results
stem:
Strips of materials X and Y were tested. The results are shown.

Which statement is correct?
figure:
MaterialLoad testBend test
Xheld the load without breakingsnapped as soon as it was bent
Yheld the load without breakingbent without breaking
key: Read each test on its own. The load test decides strong; the bend test decides flexible.

options.text: X is not strong, because it snapped.
options.pick: X broke, and breaking sounds like being weak.
options.why: X snapped in the bend test, not the load test. It held the load, so it is strong. Snapping when bent shows it is not flexible.

options.text: Y is flexible, so it must also be waterproof.
options.pick: Y passed both tests, so it seems to be good at everything.
options.why: Waterproof was never tested. Bending tells you nothing about whether a material absorbs water.

options.text: X and Y are both strong, but only Y is flexible.
options.pick: Read each test on its own: both held the load, and only Y bent without breaking.
options.why: Holding the load without breaking means strong, so both are strong. Only Y passed the bend test, so only Y is flexible.

options.text: X and Y are both flexible, because they both held the load.
options.pick: Both did well in the load test, so it seems both would do well when bent.
options.why: The load test checks strength, not flexibility. X snapped when it was bent, so X is not flexible.

title: A swimming float
stem:
A swimming float must stay on the surface of the water and must not absorb water. Four materials were tested.

Which material is most suitable for making the float?
figure:
MaterialFloat testWater test
Jstayed near the surfaceabsorbed water, mass went up
Ksank to the bottomdid not absorb water
Lstayed near the surfacedid not absorb water
Msank to the bottomabsorbed water, mass went up
key: Floating and not absorbing water are two separate properties. The float needs both.

options.pick: List the two jobs, then find the material that passed both tests.
options.why: L stayed near the surface and did not absorb water, so it does both jobs.

options.pick: J floats, and floating looks like the main job of a float.
options.why: J absorbed water. Floating says nothing about absorbing water, and a float that soaks up water gets heavy and soggy.

options.pick: K does not absorb water, so it stays dry.
options.why: K sank. A float must stay on the surface, so K fails one of its two jobs.

options.pick: J and L both floated, so either would stay on the surface.
options.why: Floating is only one of the two jobs. J absorbed water, so only L passes both tests.

title: Which fabric absorbs the most?
stem:
Siti wants to find out which of three fabrics absorbs the most water. She soaks a piece of each fabric in water and measures its mass before and after soaking.

Which of these must she keep the same for a fair test?
key: Change only the type of material. Keep everything else that could affect the result the same. The result is what you measure.

options.pick: It is what the experiment is about, so it feels important to control.
options.why: The type of fabric is the one thing she changes on purpose. If it were kept the same, there would be nothing to compare.

options.text: The mass of each piece after soaking
options.pick: Mass is being measured, so it sounds like something to control.
options.why: The mass after soaking is the result she measures. It is expected to be different for each fabric; that is how she finds the answer.

options.pick: It is easy to keep the same, so it sounds like a fair-test answer.
options.why: Colour does not affect how much water a fabric absorbs, so keeping it the same does nothing for the test.

options.text: The size of each piece, the amount of water and the soaking time
options.pick: Ask what else could change how much water goes in, then keep all of it the same.
options.why: A bigger piece, more water or a longer soak could each make a fabric take in more water. Keeping them the same means any difference comes from the fabric.

title: A fair bending test
stem:
Ali wants to compare how flexible four materials are.

Which set-up is a fair test?
key: To compare flexibility, bend the materials. Only the type of material changes; the strips and the bending stay the same.

options.text: Strips of different thicknesses, each bent until it breaks
options.pick: Every strip gets the same action, so it feels fair.
options.why: A thick strip can snap when a thin strip of the same material bends. Different thicknesses would spoil the comparison.

options.text: Strips of the same size, each with a load hung on it
options.pick: The strips are the same size, which is what a fair test needs.
options.why: Hanging a load tests strength, not flexibility. To compare flexibility, the strips must be bent.

options.text: Strips of the same size and thickness, each bent by the same amount
options.pick: Only the type of material should change; the strips and the bending should be the same.
options.why: With the same size, thickness and amount of bending, any difference in the result must come from the material.

options.text: Strips of the same size, but the first strip is bent much more than the others
options.pick: The strips are the same size, so it seems the test is already fair.
options.why: Bending one strip more than the others changes a second thing. Each strip must be bent by the same amount.

title: A bright classroom
stem:
Classroom windows are made of glass so that the room is bright during the day.

Which property of glass is being used here?
key: Match the property to the job named in the question. Here the job is letting daylight in.

options.text: It lets most light pass through.
options.pick: The job named is keeping the room bright, so look for the property about light.
options.why: Glass lets most light pass through, so daylight enters the room.

options.pick: Windows keep the rain out, so waterproof is something glass is good at.
options.why: True, but the question asks about keeping the room bright. That job uses the light property, not waterproof.

options.pick: Windows have to survive wind and knocks, so strength matters.
options.why: Strength matters for a window, but it does not make the room bright. Match the property to the job named in the question.

options.pick: Glass snaps when it is bent, which is a real property of glass.
options.why: That is true of glass, but it does nothing to brighten the room.

title: A lunch box lid
stem:
A lunch box lid must let you see the food inside without opening it, and must not break when another box is stacked on top. Four materials were tested.

Which material is most suitable for the lid?
figure:
MaterialLight testLoad test
Plet most light throughbroke under the load
Qlet most light throughheld the load without breaking
Rlet no light throughheld the load without breaking
Slet some light throughheld the load without breaking
key: List both jobs, then check every material against both. The most suitable one passes both clearly.

options.pick: P lets most light through, so you can see the food clearly.
options.why: P broke under the load, so it fails the second job.

options.pick: R is strong, and a lid that gets things stacked on it needs to be strong.
options.why: R lets no light through, so you could not see the food at all.

options.pick: S is strong and you can still see a little through it.
options.why: S only lets some light through, so the food would be hard to see. Q does both jobs fully.

options.pick: List both jobs, then pick the material that passed both tests.
options.why: Q lets most light through and held the load without breaking.
